title: When would you use a Web Worker?
description: Off-main-thread computation: the message-passing model, structured cloning of payloads, SharedArrayBuffer, and when workers don't help.

data.text: **Question:** When would you use a Web Worker?

Use a Web Worker when you have **CPU-heavy JavaScript that would block the main thread** and freeze the UI: parsing large JSON/CSV, crypto/hashing, image/video processing (e.g., pixel manipulation), compression, search/indexing over big datasets, complex calculations in editors or games. A worker runs in a **separate thread with its own event loop** — it has no DOM access, and communication happens only via `postMessage` (structured-cloned payloads) or `SharedArrayBuffer`. The main thread stays responsive. The trade-off: message serialization cost and code complexity, so a worker only pays off when the compute is substantial or the work can be backgrounded (prefetching, speculative indexing).

**The model:**
- `const w = new Worker('/worker.js')` — loads and runs a script on another thread; module workers via `{ type: 'module' }` support import/export
- `w.postMessage(data)` — data is **structured-cloned** (deep copy across threads; functions/DOM nodes can't be cloned — those throw)
- `w.onmessage = (e) => ...` receives results; `w.terminate()` kills the thread
- Inside the worker: `self.onmessage`, `self.postMessage`; workers can spawn nested workers and use fetch, IndexedDB, timers
- **Transferables**: ArrayBuffers can move (not copy) ownership via `postMessage(buf, [buf])` — zero-copy, ideal for large binary payloads; the sender's buffer becomes detached
- **SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics**: true shared memory with atomic ops — used by codecs/WASM; requires cross-origin isolation headers (COOP/COEP)

**Practical integration patterns:**
- **Request/response**: main sends jobs with ids; worker replies with { id, result } — like a tiny RPC
- **Comlink / promise-based wrappers**: libraries that hide postMessage plumbing behind async function calls
- **Framework hooks**: React-heavy compute (big filter/sort/search index) in a worker with useSyncExternalStore or a small state bridge; TanStack Query v5 has experimental worker integration
- **Lazy worker**: create on first heavy task so initial page load isn't taxed

**When it doesn't help:**
- DOM work — workers can't touch the DOM; layout/render stays on main anyway
- Small tasks — clone + round-trip overhead exceeds the compute
- Frequent tiny messages — batch instead
- Simple async latency (network) — that's promises, not workers

**Alternatives to know:** `requestIdleCallback` for low-priority scheduling, WASM for numeric-heavy loops (can run inside a worker), OffscreenCanvas (canvas rendering in a worker), service workers (network interception — different thing entirely).

data.title: A CSV-parsing worker with transferables
Workers don't make work go away
data.text: They move it off the thread the user is waiting on. If the result still needs to become DOM (rendering 100k rows), the main thread pays there instead — pair workers with virtualization or incremental rendering, and batch messages so you don't drown the bridge in clones.

Interviewers want to assess:
- The trigger: sustained CPU-bound JS that freezes interaction (with concrete examples)
- Message-passing model: structured clone cost, transferables, no DOM access
- Honesty about when workers don't help (DOM, small tasks, network waits)
- Awareness of the wider toolbox: WASM, OffscreenCanvas, requestIdleCallback, service worker ≠ web worker

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Web Worker: separate thread, own event loop, no DOM — for CPU-heavy JS
postMessage structured-clones payloads; transferables move buffers zero-copy
Cost model: batching matters; small tasks aren't worth the bridge
Workers complement, not replace: virtualize the rendering, WASM for numeric loops
data.takeaway: A worker is the browser's 'do this somewhere else' button — press it for sustained computation that would freeze interaction, and count the serialization cost before you do.
